messages.author: 49e107cb0f8a3d27
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
Hi Marmaduke,

great question. There’s been a lot of recent work that extends beyond this framework. In general, using a mixture of Gaussians as an approximation makes it very difficult to optimize in a robust and easily accessible manner (e.g., how many mixtures, does nonparametrics make sense, is the computation efficient?). Rajesh Ranganath, David Blei, and I are working on a very similar idea that uses recent tricks from the literature. It extends the variational model to arbitrary mean-field distributions + prior. This means you can fit both discrete and continuous latent variable models, and the approximation can be made as accurate as you want it to be.

It should go up on arXiv soon, and we’re all (Alp included) excited about its future for ADVI.

Best,
Dustin

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
One more comment:

I think the main challenge to implementing NPV in Stan is that it makes use of the diagonal of the Hessian of the log-posterior. There are ways to compute or approximate this efficiently, but none are implemented in Stan at the moment (to my knowledge).

In any case, Dustin's points are quite relevant; in particular, NPV only optimizes an approximate bound (in general), and in very high dimensions the benefits to using a mixture diminish, since it gets harder to fill up the space with Gaussians. I'm excited to see what Dustin, Rajesh, and Dave come up with as an alternative :)

Matt

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
We do not have an efficient way to compute just the diagonal
of the Hessian. The fastest would probably be N passes of
fvar<fvar<double>> forward-mode autodiff. That'd be O(N^2),
because there are O(N) passes and each log posterior will
presumably cost O(N) [it'll be worse for models like dense GPs].

How's the diagonal then used?

This is an issue for Riemannian HMC with the diagonal
Hessian approximation. There, the motivation is in part to avoid
all the solver cost on the N x N matrix, and compared to O(N^3),
O(N^2) doesn't look so bad (N passes which assume the
log posterior calc is itself O(N)).

- Bob

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
At a high level, the diagonal in NPV is used to do a sort of approximate Laplace approximation.

The only way I know of to efficiently automatically compute the diagonal of the Hessian is using repeated symbolic differentiation; there may be a way to do it with reverse-mode automatic differentiation, but if so it'll be pretty hairy.

BTW, for a lot of models (e.g., GLMs) the cost of computing the Hessian is O(MN^2), where M is the number of observations; if M>N, then there's not much point in worrying about the O(N^3) cost of solving a big system of equations.

Matt

fvar<fvar<double>> or fvar<var>. In fact, we have functionals

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
Multimodality is hard --- an open research problem. There
are very simple multimodalities that standard approaches
can sample through all the modes for, some multimodalities which
are just nuisances, and then some special algorithms which can handle
limited multimodality. Nothing can handle combinatorial multimodality
of the kind you get in models like LDA or Ising systems --- non-parametric
generalizations only make matters worse combinatorially.

- Bob

messages.author: 3d643362f888e7df
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
On 10/14/2015 07:28 PM, Alp Kucukelbir wrote:
> could you share some more details about your nonlinear dynamical systems
> model?

It's a model of a network of nonlinear oscillators with linear additive
noise, coupled with a given connectivity matrix. Observations are a
linear combination of the state variables. We encode the model like a
autoregressive process, with a Euler-Maruyama discretization of the SDE,
something like

data {
matrix[N, N] weights;
matrix[S, N] gain;
matrix[T, S] Z;
real dt;
}
parameters {
matrix[T, N] X, Y;
}
model {
vector[N] input;

for (t in 1:(T-1)) {
input <- weights * X[t]';
X[t+1] ~ normal(X[t] + dt * dXdt(X[t], Y[t], input), sig);
Y[t+1] ~ normal(Y[t] + dt * dYdt(X[t], Y[t]), sig);
Z[t+1] ~ normal(gain*X[t+1]', eps);
}
}

where d{X,Y}dt are functions defining the differential equations, N is
around 15 network nodes, and the current dataset has T=1000 time points,
so the number of hidden states is in the tens of thousands. Still, we
are seeing somewhat plausible results with the mean-field algorithm in a
few minutes.

> were you able to try it with the "fullrank" version of the algorithm
> (assuming your model/dataset is small?)

It runs, but slow (10s of seconds / iter) and memory intensive (~ 8gb).
I didn't wait for it to finish so I don't know if this is worth doing or
not. FWIW, NUTS/HMC spends hours and hours warming up on the same model
& data.

At least for the sequence of hidden states, one would expect short-time
correlation, so this made me wonder if some comprise between full rank
and diagonal is possible, i.e. a banded or sparse covariance?

messages.author: 453ddfeccaf29bbb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Nonparametric variational inference
parts:
hi marmaduke,

that's a very interesting model.

do you remember what value of eta you used? i wonder if mean-field
might give you some more reasonable answers with a smaller value for
eta. (it'll take more iterations to converge, of course.) [we will be
releasing an auto-tuning feature for eta soon.]

i'd also be curious to see how fullrank does on a subset of the data.
(maybe the first T=100 points?) we found fullrank to perform really
well in the stochastic volatility model from the Stan manual, while
meanfield struggled to capture some aspects of the model.

we're very interested in structured covariance matrix approximations,
such as low-rank, sparse, banded, etc. i don't believe we have a
schedule for when we'll get around to exploring these options, but do
let us know if you'd be interested in implementing and/or playing
around with them!

cheers
alp
